'''''Cocker's Arithmetick''''', also known by its full title '''''"Cocker's Arithmetick: Being a Plain and Familiar Method Suitable to the Meanest Capacity for the Full Understanding of That Incomparable Art, As It Is Now Taught by the Ablest School-Masters in City and Country"''''', is a [[grammar school]] [[mathematics]] textbook written by the English [[engraver]] and teacher [[Edward Cocker]] (1631–1676) and published posthumously by John Hawkins in 1678.<ref>{{cite book | title=Cocker's Arithmetick: Item Details | via=WorldCat | year=2008 | oclc=34162097 }}</ref><ref name=yeldham>{{cite book | last=Yeldham | first=Florence | title=The Teaching of Arithmetic Through Four Hundred Years (1535-1935) | pages=75, 80, 80–83, 85 | location=London | publisher=George G. Harrap & Co. Ltd. | year=1936 | oclc=152432557}}</ref> ''Arithmetick'' along with companion volume, ''[[Decimal Arithmetick]]'' published in 1684, were used to teach mathematics in schools in the United Kingdom for more than 150 years.

==Disputed authorship==
Some controversy exists over the authorship of the book.  [[Augustus De Morgan]] claimed the work was written by Hawkins, who merely used Cocker's name to lend the authority of his reputation to the book.<ref name=yeldham/>  Ruth Wallis, in 1997, wrote an article in ''[[Annals of Science]]'', claiming De Morgan's analysis was flawed and Cocker was the real author.<ref>R Wallis, Edward Cocker (1632?-1676) and his arithmetick: De Morgan demolished, Ann. of Sci. 54 (1997), 507-522.</ref>

==Popularity and impact==
The popularity of ''Arithmetick'' is unquestioned by its more than 130 editions, and that its place was woven in the fabric of the popular culture of the time is evidenced by its references in the phrase, "according to Cocker", meaning "absolutely correct" or "according to the rules".<ref>{{MacTutor|id=Cocker|title=Edward Cocker}}</ref> Such noted figures of history as [[Benjamin Franklin]] and [[Thomas Simpson]] are documented as having used the book.<ref>{{cite book | last=Franklin  | first=Benjamin  | chapter=Chapter One | title=The Private Life of the Late Benjamin Franklin, LL.D. Originally Written By Himself, And Now Translated From The French (The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin) | location=London | publisher=Printed for J. Parsons, no. 21, Pater-Noster Row | year=1793 | oclc=4886899 | url=https://www.earlyamerica.com/lives/franklin/chapt1/ | quote=And now it was that, being on some occasion made asham'd of my ignorance in figures, which I had twice failed in learning when at school, I took Cocker's book of Arithmetick, and went through the whole by myself with great ease | accessdate=2008-07-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last=Ball | first=W. W. Rouse | edition=Fourth | title=A Short Account of the History of Mathematics | location=New York | publisher=Dover Publications | year=1960 | oclc=220957321 | url=https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/HistMath/People/Simpson/RouseBall/RB_Simpson.html | accessdate=2008-07-17}}</ref> Over 100 years after its publication, [[Samuel Johnson]] carried a copy of ''Arithmetick'' on his tour of Scotland, and mentions it in his letters:
:''In the afternoon tea was made by a very decent girl in a printed linen; she engaged me so much, that I made her a present of Cocker's Arithmetick.''<ref>{{cite book | last=Johnson | first=Samuel | title=Letters of Samuel Johnson | url=https://archive.org/details/lettersofsamuelj01john | location=Oxford | publisher=Clarendon Press | year=1892 | oclc=61918137}}</ref>

==Writing style==
Though popular, like most texts of its time, ''Arithmetick's'' style is formal, stiff and difficult to follow as illustrated in its explanation of the "[[Rule of three (mathematics)|rule of three]]".
{{blockquote|Again, observe, that of the three given numbers, those two that are of the same kind, one of them must be the first, and the other the third, and that which is of the same kind with the number sought, must be the second number in the rule of three; and that you may know which of the said numbers to make your first, and which your third, know this, that to one of those two numbers there is always affixed a demand, and that number upon which the demand lieth must always be reckoned the third number}}

As well as the rule of three, ''Arithmetick'' contains instructions on [[alligation]] and the [[rule of false position]]. Following the common practice of textbooks at the time, each rule is illustrated with numerous examples of commercial transactions involving the exchange of wheat, rye and other seeds; calculation of costs for the erection of houses and other structures; and the rotation of gears on a shaft.<ref name=yeldham/> The text contains the earliest known use of the term ''[[lowest terms]]''.<ref>{{cite web | author=Jeff Miller | title=Earliest Known Uses of Some of the Words of Mathematics: 'Lowest Terms' | url=https://members.aol.com/jeff570/l.htm | work=Jeff Miller's Mathword | date=28 April 2008 | accessdate=2008-07-17}}</ref><!--

==''Decimal Arithmetick''==
''Decimal Arithmetick'' was published in 1685 as a companion to ''Arithmetick''. The concept of decimal fractions and the advantages of using them in calculations were well known, but a wide variety of different notations were in use.<ref>[http://members.aol.com/jeff570/fractions.html ''Earliest Uses of Symbols for Fractions''] by Jeff Miller</ref> After surveying various notations, ''Decimal Arithmetick'' recommends the [[decimal point]] notation introduced by [[John Napier]]:

:''A decimal fraction being written ... by having a point or prick prefixed before it ... being written according to the first direction, I conceive they may be most fit for calculation.''<ref name=yeldham/>

''Decimal Arithmetick'' gives instructions for calculations involving decimals, methods of extracting roots, and an overview of the concept of logarithms. There are many worked examples, some of which involve solid geometry or the calculation of interest.
